records.story: Booker Noe (1929 to 2004), Jim Beam's grandson, ran the distilling at Jim Beam for more than forty years and liked his bourbon as it came out of the barrel. As the house tells it, he chose barrels from the middle floors of the rackhouse, where the heat and the damp suit long ageing, and bottled them uncut and unfiltered, at whatever strength they had reached. In 1987 he gave such bottlings to friends as holiday gifts under the name Booker's True Barrel Bourbon, and in 1988 Booker's went on public sale. In 1992 Beam gathered it with Baker's, Basil Hayden's and Knob Creek as its Small Batch Bourbon Collection. He laid barrels down to the end: rye he filled in 2003, the year before his death, came out in 2016 as Booker's Rye. Since about 2015 each batch has carried a name, often drawn from his life, his home town of Springfield or his sayings, beside the year and number on the label. For a bartender, Booker's is where barrel proof is taught: one recipe, no water after the barrel, and a strength that changes with every batch, so the label in the hand is the one figure to quote.

records.story: George T. Stagg (1835 to 1893) was a Kentuckian who sold whiskey in St. Louis and bought barrels of O.F.C. bourbon from Colonel E. H. Taylor Jr. When Taylor fell into debt, Stagg took over the O.F.C. distillery in Frankfort in 1878, moving from selling whiskey to making it. In 1904, eleven years after his death, the distillery took his name as the George T. Stagg Distillery. By the distillery's account it was one of six allowed to bottle whiskey for medicine through Prohibition, and Old Stagg became the bourbon it led with as Prohibition ended. The site was renamed Buffalo Trace in 1999, and its Antique Collection began in 2000. George T. Stagg joined the collection in 2002: barrels of the corn led Mash Bill No. 1, left fifteen years and more in new charred oak and bottled uncut and unfiltered in the autumn release. Over those summers each barrel gives more than half its volume to the air, and the strength left behind goes into the bottle, so the proof is written on by hand. For a bartender it is the long end of the barrel proof lesson: the same uncut idea as any batch, carried through fifteen years, and a bottle always poured with water beside it.

records.story: The name goes back to the distillery's past: by Buffalo Trace's account, Old Stagg was the bourbon the George T. Stagg Distillery led with as Prohibition ended, and the barrel proof bourbons that carry the name grew from it. George T. Stagg itself had been an autumn release of the Antique Collection since 2002, fifteen years and more in oak. In 2013 Buffalo Trace added a younger bourbon from the same Mash Bill No. 1 and called it Stagg Jr. Its opening batch was drawn from barrels of eight to nine years and bottled uncut and unfiltered, and the distillery meant to release several batches a year rather than one. The batches were numbered as they came, and the fifteenth was released in 2020. In 2022 the Jr. left the label and the bourbon became plain Stagg, its batches marked from then on by the year and a letter, as 22A. For a bartender the two bottles side by side teach what time does to barrel proof: one recipe, one uncut bottling, about half the years in wood for Stagg, and a proof to read off each batch's label rather than recall.

records.story: The distillery behind the label stands at Bardstown, where a distillery was founded in 1879. In 2002 it brought out a small batch bourbon named for 1792, the year Kentucky became a state, at first as Ridgewood Reserve 1792. Brown-Forman, the maker of Woodford Reserve, sued over the name and the bottle, a federal judge ruled for it in 2004, and the bourbon became 1792 Ridgemont Reserve, later simply 1792. In 2009 the Sazerac Company bought the distillery and its brands from Constellation Brands, and the site took the name Barton 1792 Distillery. Full Proof followed in 2016. By the brand's account it is bottled at 125 proof, the strength at which its spirit went into new oak years before, and it skips chill filtering for a plate and frame filter. Reviewers note that the bourbon leaves the barrel stronger and is brought back down to 125, so it is full proof, not barrel proof. For a bartender it is the plain lesson in the words on a strong label: barrel proof, cask strength, entry proof and full proof are four promises, and of the four, barrel proof and cask strength alone say the whiskey reached the bottle as it left the barrel.

records.table: Barrell Bourbon is the Louisville blender's numbered series of straight bourbons bought from Tennessee, Kentucky and Indiana, married and bottled at cask strength without chill filtering. Each batch is its own bourbon, with its own ages and proof, so read the label before you describe it.
records.story: Barrell Craft Spirits was founded in Louisville in 2013 by a founder who had made his career, by the house's account, in marketing and technology. It began as a blender and bottler, not a distiller: it bought aged straight bourbon, chose and married the barrels, and bottled the blend at the strength the barrels gave, without chill filtering, under a batch number. Rye, blended whiskey and rum followed in the same way, Barrell Whiskey among them in 2015. The bourbon batches grew more involved as the numbers rose: barrels of five to sixteen years from Tennessee, Kentucky and Indiana in one batch or another, high rye and high corn recipes married together, and a mash bill derived for the whole. In 2024 Batch 036 brought a new label that names on its front the states the whiskey came from and the age of every whiskey in the blend. For a bartender, Barrell Bourbon is barrel proof as a blender's choice rather than a distiller's: the strength is the barrels', the recipe is the blend, and the batch number is the bourbon, so a guest is told what this bottle holds and never what an earlier batch held.
